paras.text: Masonry, Roofing, Siding and Exterior Finishes, Audio Lecture

This chapter is worth about twenty two questions on your trade exam. Nine on masonry, seven on roofing, three on siding, and a few more from the finishes category. It all comes from the twenty fifteen Michigan Residential Code and standard trade practice.

This chapter has more trap pairs in it than any other, numbers that sit one apart or rules that look interchangeable. Thirty two and thirty three. Two inches and one inch. Sixteen and eight versus twenty and twelve. So every time I give you a pair, stop and say both halves out loud with the thing each one belongs to. That habit is what protects the points.
We will go in build order. Mortar, then veneer, then the fireplace and chimney, then the roof, then siding and finishes.
Idea one. The four mortars, ranked, and why strongest is the wrong instinct.
There are four mortar types, and you rank them strongest to weakest as M, S, N, O. The trick is the word masonwork. Take every other letter and you get M, S, N, O.
Type M is twenty five hundred p s i, and it goes below grade. Foundations, retaining walls, anything touching earth.
Type S is eighteen hundred p s i, the structural workhorse at or above grade.
Type N is seven hundred fifty p s i, general purpose. And here is the one the exam is really asking about, Type N is the standard choice for brick veneer above grade.
Type O is three hundred fifty p s i, for interior non load bearing work and for repointing old soft masonry only.

Now hear the reasoning, because it is the whole question. Do not reach for Type M just because it is strongest. Strongest is not what is being asked. Application is. Mortar that is harder than the brick around it will damage the brick instead of protecting it, which is exactly why old soft masonry gets Type O.

And keep grout separate from mortar in your head. They are different products with different jobs. Grout is fluid, at least two thousand p s i, and it gets poured into the block cells around the rebar. Mortar is stiff, goes between the units in bed and head joints, and those joints are typically three eighths of an inch.
Question. What mortar for brick veneer above grade, and what mortar below grade.
Type N for veneer above grade. Type M below grade. If you answered Type M for the veneer because it is strongest, that is exactly the trap.
Idea two. Masonry weather rules.
Cold weather masonry kicks in below forty degrees.

Between twenty and forty degrees, you heat the mixing water and sand so the mortar sits between forty and one hundred twenty degrees when you use it, and you protect the finished work for twenty four hours.
Below twenty degrees, no laying at all without a heated enclosure.
And burn this one in, because it is an absolute. Antifreeze in mortar is never allowed. Never, at any temperature, for any reason.
Hot weather rules trigger above one hundred degrees, or above ninety degrees with wind over eight miles an hour. Then you shade the materials, dampen absorptive brick, and fog spray the work.
Mixed mortar has a board life of about two and a half hours, and you can retemper it once inside that window. Once.

One vocabulary item that shows up. Efflorescence is that white powdery salt stain on masonry. It means water is moving through the wall, dissolving salts, and leaving them behind when it evaporates. So the answer to an efflorescence question is never a cleaner. You fix the water, meaning flashing and weeps. The stain is a symptom.
Idea three. Brick veneer, where the numbers get dense.
The air space between the veneer and the sheathing is one inch minimum, four and a half inches maximum.
The veneer hangs on wall ties, and each tie can support no more than two point six seven square feet of wall. Spacing is thirty two inches on center horizontally and twenty four inches vertically.
Hear the pattern so you do not flip them. The bigger number, thirty two, runs horizontally along the course. Corrugated ties are twenty two gauge, seven eighths of an inch wide.
Weep holes go in the first course, immediately above the flashing, at a maximum of thirty three inches on center, and at least three sixteenths of an inch in diameter.
Now the nasty pair. Ties are thirty two. Weeps are thirty three. Weeps get the extra inch. There is no logic to help you there, so just say it twice, ties thirty two, weeps thirty three.
Lintels over veneer openings. A three by three by quarter inch steel angle spans up to six feet, with four inches of bearing at each end.
And the principle underneath all of it, veneer carries only its own weight. Never floor loads, never roof loads. It is a rain jacket made of brick.

Behind every siding and veneer is the water resistive barrier, number fifteen felt or an approved housewrap, lapped two inches horizontally and six inches at vertical joints, always upper over lower, shingle fashion.
Two and six. That pair shows up on exams, and shingle fashion is the reason for both, water always runs over a lap, never into one.
Idea four. Which joint goes in which wall.
This one is easy if you learn the movement instead of the joint.
Clay brick expands over its life as it absorbs moisture. So brick walls get expansion joints, with compressible filler for the brick to push into.
Concrete block shrinks as it cures. So block walls get control joints, which give the shrinkage a planned place to crack.
Brick grows, block shrinks. Opposite movements, opposite joints.

Reinforcement basics. Number four rebar in the grouted cells for typical residential work, and nine gauge ladder wire in the bed joints every sixteen inches, which is every other course of eight inch block.
Idea five. The fireplace, which is a cluster of numbers worth real points.
The firebox. Walls are ten inches of solid masonry, or eight inches total when lined with two inches of firebrick. Firebox depth is twenty inches minimum.

The hearth. The hearth slab is four inches thick. The hearth extension out in front is two inches thick, and it can drop to three eighths of an inch if the firebox opening is raised at least eight inches above it.
The extension size depends on the size of the opening, and this is a pair.
Opening under six square feet, the extension runs sixteen inches in front and eight inches to each side.
Opening six square feet or bigger, twenty inches in front and twelve to each side.
Sixteen and eight, or twenty and twelve. The bigger fire throws sparks farther.
Clearance to combustibles around the fireplace is two inches at the front faces and sides, and four inches at the back.
The damper sits at least eight inches above the top of the opening.

And the whole assembly sits on a footing at least twelve inches thick, extending six inches beyond the face on all sides, and going down below Michigan's forty two inch frost depth. There is that number again.
Question. Fireplace opening is seven square feet. How far does the hearth extension run in front and to the sides.
Twenty inches in front and twelve to each side, because it is six square feet or larger. Sixteen and eight is the smaller opening.
Idea six. The chimney, and the three two ten rule.
Chimney height is the famous three two ten rule, and you need all of it, not part of it.
At least three feet above the highest point where the chimney passes through the roof. And at least two feet higher than any part of the building within ten feet horizontally.
Both conditions, always. Not whichever is easier.
The crown on top slopes at least ten degrees, is two inches thick at the edge, and overhangs two inches.
Flue sizing is a ratio of the fireplace opening area, and there are three ratios.
A round flue needs one twelfth of the opening area. A square or rectangular flue under a two to one shape needs one tenth. And a skinny rectangle at two to one or more needs one eighth.
Work one. A thirty six by thirty inch opening is one thousand eighty square inches. Divided by twelve, a round flue needs ninety square inches.
Notice the direction, the skinnier and less efficient the flue shape, the bigger the fraction of the opening it needs.
Chimney clearance to combustibles. Two inches for a chimney inside the house or in an exterior wall. One inch for a chimney built entirely outside the walls.

Read that split carefully, because the wrong answer is designed to sound better. The split is interior versus exterior. It is not below the roof versus above the roof, no matter how tempting that choice looks.

And the last chimney item, a cricket. That is the little diverter roof on the uphill side, and it is required when the chimney is more than thirty inches wide parallel to the ridge and does not intersect the ridge.
Question. Chimney passes through the roof, and there is a gable wall eight feet away that stands two feet higher than the chimney top. Are you compliant.
No. Three feet above the penetration is only half the rule. You also need two feet above any part of the building within ten feet horizontally, and that wall is inside ten feet.
Idea seven. Asphalt shingles and the ice barrier.
Asphalt shingles need a slope of at least two in twelve, and there is a middle band with its own rule.
From two in twelve up to four in twelve, you must run double underlayment, a nineteen inch starter and thirty six inch sheets lapped nineteen inches. Four in twelve and steeper takes a single layer.
Fasteners are twelve gauge roofing nails with three eighths inch heads, driven at least three quarters of an inch into the sheathing. The code minimum is four nails per strip shingle.
Note that carefully. Six nails is a manufacturer or high wind spec, not the code floor. If the question asks for the code minimum, it is four.
Now the ice barrier, which is the most Michigan roofing rule there is.
The ice barrier membrane runs from the lowest edge of the roof to at least twenty four inches inside the exterior wall line.

Inside the wall line. Not twenty four inches up from the eave. That distinction is the whole question, and it has a real consequence, a big overhang means a lot more membrane, because the measurement starts from the wall, not the edge.
On roofs eight in twelve or steeper, it is at least thirty six inches measured along the slope. And the only exemption is a detached accessory building with no conditioned space.
Idea eight. Flashing, and the sequencing trap.
Drip edge extends a quarter inch below the sheathing, two inches back onto the deck, and laps two inches piece to piece.
Now the sequencing trap, and it is one of the best questions on the exam because it sounds inconsistent until you understand it.
At the eaves, underlayment goes over the drip edge. At the rakes, drip edge goes over the underlayment.
Why. At the eave, water running down the underlayment has to get out on top of the metal. At the rake, wind driven water has to be kept from getting under the edge. Different threat, different order.

Step flashing where a roof meets a sidewall is four by four minimum. And at the bottom of that run you need a kickout flashing to throw the water into the gutter instead of behind the siding. In Michigan that kickout is the difference between a dry wall and a rotten one, and it is the most commonly missing piece of flashing in the field.
Open valley metal is twenty four inches wide.
Idea nine. Low slope minimums, and reroofing.
Quick and clean, these are just memory.

Standing seam metal, a quarter in twelve. Lapped metal with sealant, half in twelve. Without sealant, three in twelve. Built up roofing and single ply membranes like E P D M, a quarter in twelve. Mineral surfaced roll roofing, one in twelve. Wood shingles and wood shakes both need three in twelve, and shakes get an eighteen inch wide number thirty felt interlayment between courses.
Reroofing. Tear off is mandatory in three situations. When the deck is water soaked. When the old roof is shake, slate, or tile. Or when there are already two layers of anything up there.
Two layers is the ceiling. A third layer is never allowed.
Idea ten. Attic ventilation, and the Michigan wrinkle.
The base rule is one square foot of net free vent area for every one hundred fifty square feet of attic.
You can cut that to one in three hundred by either of two paths, and either path alone is enough.
Path one, a class one or two vapor retarder on the warm side of the ceiling, but only in climate zones six, seven, and eight.
Path two, put forty to fifty percent of the vent area high, within three feet of the ridge, with the rest down at the eaves.

Now the Michigan wrinkle, and this is the part a national book will get wrong for you. Southern lower Michigan is climate zone five A. So down there the vapor retarder path does not qualify, and you need the balanced high and low vents to earn the one in three hundred.
And keep one inch of clear air space between the insulation and the sheathing, using baffles. Insulation stuffed tight to the deck blocks the very airflow you just calculated.
Question. Attic in southern lower Michigan. How do you qualify for the one in three hundred ratio.
The balanced vent path only. Forty to fifty percent of the vent area within three feet of the ridge and the rest at the eaves, because zone five A does not qualify for the vapor retarder path.
Idea eleven. Siding.
Fasteners generally penetrate an inch and a quarter into sheathing and framing combined.

Vinyl siding lives or dies on movement. A twelve foot panel can move half an inch with temperature. So you center the nails in the slots, leave a thirty second of an inch under the head, and a quarter inch gap at the trim. Nail vinyl tight and it buckles, and that is a callback, not a warranty item.
Installation runs bottom up. Barrier, flashing, level starter strip, corners, J channel, then panels locking course over course.

Fiber cement laps an inch and a quarter minimum, and note that this one is a code number, not a manufacturer suggestion. Every field cut edge gets primed. The manufacturer clearances are six inches to grade and two inches to roofing.
Do not cross those wires. An inch and a quarter is the lap. Six inches is the grade clearance.
Stucco takes three coats over lath, two coats over masonry, with each coat kept moist for forty eight hours. The weep screed at the bottom sits four inches above earth or two inches above paving.
Idea twelve. Interior finishes, briefly, because a few questions come from here.

Drywall levels, one through five. Level one is tape embedded, for plenums. Level two is tape plus one coat, for garages and behind tile. Level three is two coats, for heavy texture. Level four is three coats, the standard painted wall. Level five adds a skim coat over the whole surface, and it is required for gloss or semi gloss paint and for critical lighting.
Level five is the answer whenever the question mentions shiny paint or a wall that gets raking light.

Tile. Thinset, the cement mortar, works everywhere including showers. Mastic is for dry area walls only, never wet areas and never floors. Shower tile goes over cement board with a waterproof membrane, and green board is not a wet area substrate.
Hardwood flooring runs perpendicular to the joists, blind nailed through the tongue, with a three eighths inch expansion gap at the walls.
Rapid fire recap. Breathe, and say these with me.

Mortar, M twenty five hundred, S eighteen hundred, N seven fifty, O three fifty, and veneer gets N. Grout two thousand. Air space one inch minimum. Ties, two point six seven square feet, thirty two horizontal, twenty four vertical, twenty two gauge. Weeps, thirty three on center, three sixteenths diameter, above the flashing. Lintel, three by three by a quarter, six foot span, four inch bearing. Felt laps, two horizontal, six vertical. Firebox, ten inches solid or eight with firebrick, twenty deep. Hearth four, extension two, or three eighths when raised eight. Extensions, sixteen and eight, or twenty and twelve at six square feet. Fireplace clearance, two at the front and sides, four at the back. Damper eight above the opening. Footing twelve thick, six past the face. Chimney, three feet, two feet, ten feet. Crown, ten degrees, two thick, two overhang. Flues, one twelfth round, one tenth square, one eighth skinny rectangle. Chimney clearance, two interior, one exterior. Cricket at thirty inches. Shingles, two twelve minimum, double felt below four twelve, four nails, three quarter inch penetration. Ice barrier twenty four inches inside the wall line, thirty six along the slope on steep roofs. Drip edge, quarter inch down, two onto the deck. Step flashing four by four. Valley metal twenty four. Two roof layers maximum. Vents, one fifty, or one three hundred with a vapor retarder in zone six or with forty to fifty percent high. Baffle space one inch. Siding nails penetrate an inch and a quarter. Fiber cement laps an inch and a quarter, six inches to grade. Stucco, three coats on lath, two on masonry, forty eight hour cure, screed four above earth and two above paving. Level five for gloss. Thinset in showers, never mastic.

Twenty two questions in this chapter. The pairs are what decide it, so tonight drill ties thirty two against weeps thirty three, sixteen and eight against twenty and twelve, and interior two inches against exterior one inch on the chimney. Those three pairs are where the points leak.
